::: {.hero}
# From raw reads to biological inference
<p class="lead">Reference guides for analysing RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, Hi-C and single-cell
RNA-seq data. Each one documents one way of taking the data from raw reads to interpretation, with
a ready-to-run Snakemake pipeline, the reasoning behind each choice, and the main alternatives.</p>
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Status
All R code in the guides has been run and tested. The RNA-seq and ChIP/ATAC pipelines have been
run end to end on simulated data; none has yet been run on a full-size real dataset. See [About](about.qmd) for what was checked and
how to report problems.
:::

## What these guides are

A record of one practitioner's workflow for each assay, written up so others can follow,
compare and adapt it. They are **a reference, not an authoritative standard**: other valid
approaches exist, and the right choices depend on your data. Where a common alternative exists, the
guides name it. Check each tool's own documentation before relying on a setting.

They are written for researchers who have (or are planning) a sequencing experiment. You don't
have to be a bioinformatician. If you can use a terminal and have met R before, you can follow
them.

## What each guide covers

- Experimental design: replicates, depth, controls and batches.
- Turning raw FASTQ files into analysis-ready data with a reproducible pipeline that runs on a
  workstation or an HPC cluster.
- Data quality at every step, using named metrics with thresholds from published standards.
- A commonly used statistical analysis for the assay, and when an alternative may suit better.
- The figures that test a conclusion, and how to read them.
- Comparing across species (liftOver, consensus genomes, outgroup logic).

## How every guide is organised

| Step | What it covers | Question it addresses |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Design | Replicates, depth, controls, confounders | *Can this experiment answer my question?* |
| 2. Raw-read QC | FastQC / MultiQC | *Is the sequencing usable?* |
| 3. Processing | Run `pipelines/<assay>` | *What did each step do to my data?* |
| 4. Processed-data QC | Assay-specific metrics | *Did the assay work?* |
| 5. Sample-level QC | PCA, correlation, outliers | *Do replicates agree? Is there batch?* |
| 6. Statistics | One commonly used test, plus alternatives | *What changed, and how confident am I?* |
| 7. Visualisation | The plots that test the result | *Does the result look right?* |
| 8. Interpretation | Annotation, enrichment | *What does it mean biologically?* |
| 9. Inference | Pros/cons, pitfalls | *What can I claim, and what can't I?* |
| 10. Cross-species extension | liftOver, consensus genome | *How do I compare species?* |

## Before you start

1. **Software:** follow [Getting started](guides/00-getting-started.md) to install conda and
   Snakemake. The pipelines create their own tool environments.
2. **Hardware:** a 16-core / 64 GB workstation is enough for most assays. HPC users can run the
   same pipelines through a Snakemake executor.
3. **Data:** use your own, or the open example data below.

## Example data

The R code in each guide runs on public example datasets that Bioconductor downloads for you.
For trying the processing pipelines, an openly available comparative study of primate
astrocytes (Ciuba *et al.* 2025, *Cell Stem Cell*, [doi:10.1016/j.stem.2024.12.011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.stem.2024.12.011))
provides RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq and Hi-C from human, chimpanzee and macaque cells
(ArrayExpress E-MTAB-13252 to 13259). Its results appear in the guides as examples of what each
analysis produces.
